executable.help:
Guffin - native GGUF chat on Metal

Usage: guffin -m MODEL [options]
       guffin inspect MODEL

Chat is the default. Give a prompt for one answer and exit.
Chat shows prompt/generation rates and internal TTFT after each reply.

  -m, --model FILE          Model GGUF (or use positional MODEL)
  -p, --prompt TEXT         Answer TEXT once, then exit
  -n, --max-new-tokens N    Optional reply token limit
  -c, --context-size N      Context capacity in tokens
      --draft-model FILE    Enable lossless speculative decoding
      --temperature T       Sampling temperature (default: 0.8)
      --greedy              Select the most likely token
      --seed N              Sampling seed (default: random)
      --stats               Also show timing for one-shot/piped output
  -h, --help                Show this help
      --help-all            Include advanced options
      --version             Show build identity

Examples:
  guffin -m models/gemma-3-12b-it-Q4_K_M.gguf
  guffin -m MODEL --draft-model DRAFT
  guffin -m MODEL -p "Explain unified memory" -n 128

Review the following two project documents as a new contributor. Explain the architecture, the boundary between production execution and experimental evidence, and three important correctness contracts. Identify stated limitations. Ground your answer in the documents and keep it under 350 words. # Guffin **Native Gemma inference for a fanless Mac.** Guffin is a C++20 and Metal GGUF engine for local chat on a **16 GiB MacBook Air M4**. It owns the path from model loading and tokenization to GPU kernels, conversation caches and sampling. **Gemma 3 12B** is the main target, with a native **Gemma 3 270M** speculative drafter. **Gemma 2 9B** remains supported. The project investigates what makes complete chat faster on a constrained machine. Its experiments focus on weight traffic, cache memory and proposal verification. The resulting design reuses useful target work and keeps ownership explicit; the [retrospective](docs/SPECULATIVE_DECODING_RETROSPECTIVE.md) records which ideas survived, which failed and what those results actually establish. [Run](#quick-start) · [Architecture](#inside-the-engine) · [Speculation](#how-h1-reuses-target-work) · [Lessons](#what-the-experiments-taught-us) · [Benchmarks](#performance) · [Code map](docs/GRAPH.md) ## Quick start The tested setup is M4 / 16 GiB, macOS 26.6.2 and Apple clang 21. Install the Xcode Command Line Tools if needed with `xcode-select --install`, then: ```sh git clone https://github.com/Coach6/guffin.git cd guffin make -j4 install ``` Download the [tested Gemma 3 12B Q4_K_M GGUF][target-model] into `models/`. Chat is the default: ```sh guffin -m models/gemma-3-12b-it-Q4_K_M.gguf ``` For native lossless speculation, also put the [supported 270M Q8_0 drafter][draft-model] in `models/`: ```sh guffin -m models/gemma-3-12b-it-Q4_K_M.gguf \ --draft-model models/gemma-3-270m-it-Q8_0.gguf ``` The installed command works from any directory; model paths may be relative or absolute. Installation selects `/opt/homebrew/bin` when present, otherwise `/usr/local/bin`. For a custom location, use `make install PREFIX="$HOME/.local"` and add `$HOME/.local/bin` to `PATH`. Metal source is embedded in the executable; installed inference needs no checkout assets, Python environment or network. ## Inside the engine The CLI handles interaction. The session owns conversation behavior and prepared plans; those plans own weights, key/value (KV) caches and scratch buffers. Both target and drafter execute natively on Metal; final target sampling runs on the CPU. ```mermaid flowchart TD CLI["CLI
commands, streaming, metrics"] -->|session API| S["Chat session
history, context, stopping"] G["GGUF + tokenizer"] -->|validate and prepare| P["Prepared plans
weights, KV, scratch"] S -->|execute| T["Gemma target on Metal
prefill, decode, verification"] S -. optional pairing .-> D["270M drafter on Metal
proposal and probability law"] P -->|resources| T P -->|resources| D T -->|compact candidates| A["CPU target sampler
filters, RNG, lossless correction"] D -. proposed token .-> T D -. proposal law .-> A A -->|selected tokens| S ``` The optimization strategy removes repeated work at concrete boundaries: | Decision | What it changes | | --- | --- | | [Pack quantized weights for GPU access](include/local_gguf_engine/tensor/kquant_packing.hpp) | Prepare adjacent output columns for parallel GPU lanes. Packed Q4/Q6 two-row projections reuse weight fragments without expanding the whole model to floating point. | | [Calculate Q4 correction sums at their producers](src/engine/gemma_target_runtime.cpp) | Normalization, GELU and attention produce reusable activation sums; projections consume them without a separate launch. | | [Use prompt-sized matrix tiles](src/tensor/backends/metal/metal_command_context.mm) | Larger Gemma 3 tiles reuse decoded weights across useful prompt rows; small decode batches retain compact kernels. | | [Store target KV in F16](src/tensor/backends/metal/metal_kernels.mm) | Cached keys and values use half precision; attention accumulates in F32. Local-attention layers use bounded rings. | | [Select candidates before GPU readback](src/engine/sampling.cpp) | Transfer compact candidates for configured CPU sampling, avoiding routine full-vocabulary readback. | Fused Q4 sums serve Gemma 3 ordinary/H1 execution and Gemma 2 shared verification. Gemma 3 preserves native Q4/Q6 weights and shares its tied embedding/output-head allocation. Gemma 2's established policy requantizes Q6 down weights to Q4 and its F16 output head to Q8; those conversions change weights. [llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp) is the broader external reference. Guffin specializes selected Gemma paths for M4. Its contribution is the native layout, scheduling and state integration of established methods; current matched performance comparisons are pending. ## How H1 reuses target work Speculation helps when its complete cycle costs less per delivered token than ordinary decoding. **H1 drafts one token at a time.** It pairs the current target-selected token `r` with a proposed continuation `x`. Packed body projections can reuse fragments across those two causal rows. The diagram starts with `r` selected but awaiting its target forward pass: ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph Ordinary["Ordinary: two successive target steps"] direction LR O1["Target row r"] --> O2["Deliver r
sample x"] --> O3["Target row x"] --> O4["Deliver x
next-token candidates"] end subgraph H1["H1: one proposal, joint verification"] direction LR D["270M proposes x
conditioned on r"] --> V["Target rows r, x
share projection fragments"] --> A{"Accept x?"} A -->|Yes| K["Deliver r, x
reuse row-x candidates"] A -->|No| C["Deliver r
carry corrected token z"] end ``` On acceptance, row `x` already provides candidates for the next target-selected token. On rejection, its speculative suffix is discarded and the corrected draw becomes the next token. Selecting that token needs no extra target forward; processing and caching it happen in the next cycle. **Lossless** means preserving the configured target sampling distribution. Here `p` and `q` are the target and actual draft distributions. Acceptance uses `min(1, p(x) / q(x))`; rejection samples the normalized positive part of `p − q`. Identical seeded text is unnecessary. The algorithm follows [speculative sampling research][speculation-paper]; its engine implementation must also preserve filters, history and stopping. ## Correctness and ownership Selected private verification rows are copied into the target cache before callbacks; finalization retains the delivered prefix and restores any uncommitted suffix. Target and draft caches, sampler state and callback receipts must agree. The contracts have direct evidence routes: | Contract | Where to inspect it | | --- | --- | | Lossless probability correction and configured sampling filters | [Analytic sampling tests](tests/engine/lossless_sampling_tests.cpp) | | Packed projections, fused sums and independent F16 rounding | [Metal numerical tests](tests/tensor/gemma3_metal_tests.cpp) | | Target equations, local-cache wrap and callback/stop receipts | [Gemma 3 runtime tests](tests/engine/gemma3_target_runtime_tests.cpp) | | Tickets retain stable storage through moves, completion and rollback | [Target/verifier ownership tests](tests/engine/gemma2_metal_plan_tests.cpp) | | Descriptors are validated before allocation; views check backing storage | [Tensor admission tests](tests/tensor/tensor_tests.cpp) | Independent references, fault injection and benchmark drivers are excluded from shipping objects. Short authenticated checkpoint references pass; an independent 128-token natural-prompt comparison exceeds existing numerical bounds for an unresolved reason. The [validation boundary](docs/SPECULATIVE_DECODING_RETROSPECTIVE.md#numerical-validation-has-a-boundary) records its scope. ## What the experiments taught us - **Optimize the whole speculative cycle.** Proposal quality and verifier cost must pay for drafting and state publication together. Larger horizons did not earn a retained chat advantage in the tested configurations. - **Measure the complete conversation.** Fewer dispatches and faster isolated kernels sometimes failed to improve chat. Retained mechanisms must survive prompt processing, follow-ups, memory pressure and thermals. - **Keep the numerical target explicit.** F16 KV and Gemma 2 requantization are precision choices. Lossless speculation preserves the selected target law. Rejected runtime experiments are removed; their designs, measurements and limits remain documented in the [engineering retrospective](docs/SPECULATIVE_DECODING_RETROSPECTIVE.md). ## Performance **Release benchmarks and matched llama.cpp comparisons are pending.** Cells remain blank until the planned testing pass; `—` means pending. | Guffin mode | Prompt tok/s | Generation tok/s | Internal TTFT (ms) | First text (ms) | Peak footprint (GiB) | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Gemma 2 ordinary | — | — | — | — | — | | Gemma 2 suffix retrieval | — | — | — | — | — | | Gemma 3 ordinary | — | — | — | — | — | | Gemma 3 + 270M H1 | — | — | — | — | — | The testing pass will report pinned revisions, exact models and executed precision, context and sampler settings, timing boundaries and system state. [Performance evidence](docs/PERFORMANCE.md) keeps the measurement scope and historical development results separate from these pending release figures. ## Everyday use and support Interactive replies show prompt tokens/s, generation tokens/s and internal TTFT. Internal TTFT ends at the first selected token; first visible text is a separate boundary. Loading and startup warmup are separate from reply timings. ```sh # One answer; requested timings go to stderr guffin -m models/gemma-3-12b-it-Q4_K_M.gguf -p "Explain unified memory." -n 128 --stats # Gemma 2 chat, with default suffix retrieval guffin -m models/gemma-2-9b-Q4.gguf # Disable all speculation for ordinary Gemma 2 decoding guffin -m models/gemma-2-9b-Q4.gguf --no-speculative # Inspect metadata and tensors without inference guffin inspect models/gemma-3-12b-it-Q4_K_M.gguf ``` `/help` lists chat commands; Ctrl+C stops a reply and Ctrl+D exits at the prompt. Piped stdout contains answers. `guffin --help` lists common options; `--help-all` includes diagnostics, and `--version` reports the build identity. - **Models:** tested Gemma 3 12B IT Q4_K_M, Gemma 2 9B IT Q4_K_M and the authenticated 270M Q8_0 drafter. Matching family names or filenames alone do not establish compatibility. - **Context:** Gemma 3 defaults to 16K; `-c, --context-size` sets capacity within model/device limits. The drafter caps paired execution at 32K. The tested Gemma 2 model declares 8K. `--context-shift` drops oldest complete turns when full. - **Scope:** text-only, Metal-first inference. Release builds target M4; other devices and OS versions are unvalidated. Gemma 4 is future work. ## Development ```sh make # optimized executable make MODE=debug test # native correctness checks bash scripts/ci.sh # native and Python repository checks make release-test # optimized correctness checks make uninstall # use the installation PREFIX, if customized ``` Use [the code map](docs/GRAPH.md) to find the owning module and relevant tests. Changes should preserve its numerical, ownership and lifecycle contracts; performance claims need actual chat evidence. Optional checkpoint checks require their authenticated artifacts. [Engine principles](docs/ENGINE_PRINCIPLES.md) explain the design expectations. For help or bug reports, [open an issue](https://github.com/Coach6/guffin/issues) with your device, macOS version, `guffin --version`, model and command. Project licensing is pending selection; model downloads have their own terms. [Current state](docs/NEXT_TASK.md) records the development handoff. [target-model]: https://huggingface.co/ggml-org/gemma-3-12b-it-GGUF/blob/e5feec63a04a7a5f9b4128bf469781359d1a3b1a/gemma-3-12b-it-Q4_K_M.gguf [draft-model]: https://huggingface.co/ggml-org/gemma-3-270m-it-GGUF/blob/e7647be17ae1108f2f605ed061ca0608b171afff/gemma-3-270m-it-Q8_0.gguf [speculation-paper]: https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/leviathan23a.html # Engine Principles This file defines the project's permanent engineering and coding principles. ## Maintain the Software - Give each module a coherent responsibility and keep dependencies directed toward the component that owns the behavior. - Define contracts for shapes, precision, cache positions, committed state, cancellation and failure. Keep ownership and resource lifetimes explicit. - Keep authoritative configuration and model capabilities in one place; adapters should pass the resolved configuration rather than recreate it. - Share mechanisms when their behavior is shared. Keep architectural differences explicit and introduce abstractions when existing cases justify them. - Remove abandoned execution paths and their exclusive tests and probes after tracing callers. Preserve useful findings in documentation and history. - Keep independent numerical references, fault injection and developer probes outside the production execution dependency. - Preserve behavior and hardware costs when refactoring: review allocations, transfers, synchronization and dispatches as part of the contract. - Test observable behavior and meaningful invariants so internal structure can improve without rewriting tests merely to mirror the implementation. - Keep builds and installation reproducible from a fresh checkout. Compiler dependency tracking must cover public and private headers. ## Optimize the System - Treat end-to-end inference as the product. Optimize a subsystem only when evidence connects it to meaningful whole-path cost. - Profile before choosing work. Attribute aggregate time, dispatches, data movement, allocation, synchronization, and CPU/GPU gaps. - Estimate the maximum end-to-end gain first. If it is within run-to-run noise or does not justify the complexity, choose a larger bottleneck. - Use microbenchmarks to explain a cost, compare candidates, or validate a hypothesis. Accept a performance change only when the real production path improves under comparable conditions. - Prefer removing work, transfers, waits, allocations, and passes over making unnecessary work slightly faster. - Measure release builds on representative inputs. Warm the path, repeat runs, report variance, control thermals and system state when practical, and interleave alternatives when drift could bias the result. ## Protect the Architecture - Put behavior with the component that owns it. Make layout, lifetime, residency, synchronization, and mutation explicit at boundaries. - Keep engine semantics independent from CLI, UI, benchmark, and diagnostic concerns. Diagnostics may observe production execution; they must not become a second execution path without a strong reason. - Design the hot path for the intended hardware and workload, but keep interfaces narrow so specialization does not leak everywhere. - Specialize when measured shapes or formats justify it. Generalize only when repeated real cases reveal a stable boundary; do not build speculative layers. - Prefer the simplest design that preserves required invariants. Never trade a clear ownership model for local convenience or a small isolated win. - Make performance-sensitive state persistent when its lifetime is persistent. Avoid hidden copies, implicit format conversions, temporary allocations, and synchronization inside cheap-looking abstractions. - Complete the agreed implementation end to end. Let architecture and useful outcomes determine the scope of a change; avoid artificial iteration limits, temporary substitutes, and unnecessary approval boundaries. - Do not mix performance work with unrelated cleanup, broad refactors, or new features. Remove rejected candidates and temporary instrumentation. ## Prove Changes - Encode invariants in types, validation, ownership, and tests where practical. Treat dimensions, strides, packing, alignment, precision, aliasing, cache position, and synchronization as correctness properties. - Validate assumptions where bad data enters and fail with enough context to identify the violated model, tensor, layout, backend, or lifecycle contract. - Add deterministic tests for changed behavior and likely regressions. Cover boundary shapes, tails, precision limits, and unavailable devices as relevant. - Use a small independent reference, golden output, or parity test to validate optimized numerical code. Do not use the optimized implementation as its own oracle. - Choose tolerances from the expected numerical error and accumulation method; never loosen a tolerance merely to make a test pass. - Test the public path that owns the behavior. Unit tests isolate the mechanism; integration tests prove the system connects correctly. - Keep fallback behavior explicit. It must not silently change backend, residency, precision, or performance characteristics. - A performance change is complete only when correctness checks pass, the real benchmark improves beyond noise, and the measurements support the claimed cause. ## Comment for the Next Decision Write comments that preserve information a future reader cannot recover by reading the code alone: - why a design or algorithm was chosen over a plausible alternative; - numerical assumptions, precision choices, and acceptable error; - tensor shape, order, stride, packing, alignment, and aliasing invariants; - buffer ownership, residency, lifetime, and synchronization requirements; - hardware, backend, or API constraints and fallback behavior; - non-obvious performance tradeoffs and when they hold. Do not restate names, syntax, or obvious control flow. Prefer clearer code over comments that explain confusing code. Put a short comment before the relevant invariant or tricky block, and update or delete it with the code. Record durable design reasons, not benchmark results or a development diary. ## Before Committing to a Design Ask: 1. What measured whole-path problem does this solve? 2. What is the plausible upper bound on the end-to-end improvement? 3. Which ownership, layout, lifetime, or synchronization invariant changes? 4. Can the same result come from removing work or simplifying the data flow? 5. Is the abstraction supported by repeated cases, or only imagined future use? 6. How will correctness and real-path performance be proved independently? 7. If the idea fails, can all of its complexity be removed cleanly? If these questions do not have concrete answers, gather evidence before adding architecture.

Turn your review into a practical checklist for a contributor changing sampling or cache logic. Separate automated correctness checks from actual-chat performance measurements. Use details from the supplied documents and keep it under 250 words.

## Guffin Project Analysis

Based on the provided README.md and ENGINE_PRINCIPLES.md documents, here's a breakdown of Guffin's architecture, boundary between production execution and experimental evidence, and key correctness contracts:

**Architecture:**

- **C++20 and Metal:** Guffin is built on C++20 and leverages Apple's Metal GPU API for native inference on macOS.
- **Modular Design:** It follows a modular architecture with distinct components for the CLI, session management, prepared plans, target and drafter execution, sampling, and caching.
- **Native Inference:** Guffin performs inference entirely on the device, eliminating dependencies on external Python environments or network connections.
- **GGUF Integration:** It utilizes the GGUF (General-Purpose GPU Unified Fusion) format for model loading and tokenization, integrating with existing Gemma models.
- **Speculation:** Guffin incorporates a speculative decoding mechanism (H1) to potentially speed up inference by preemptively proposing tokens.

**Production Execution vs. Experimental Evidence:**

- **Production Path:** The core of Guffin's design focuses on the "production path" - efficient and reliable inference execution. This path is carefully documented and tested for correctness and performance.
- **Experimental Evidence:**  The project emphasizes rigorous testing and benchmarking to evaluate the effectiveness of various optimizations and architectural choices. 

    - **Numerical Validation:**  Extensive numerical tests verify the correctness of core calculations, ensuring accuracy and avoiding subtle bugs.
    - **Microbenchmarks:**  Targeted benchmarks measure specific components and operations to understand performance bottlenecks and guide optimization efforts.
    - **Release Benchmarks:**  Benchmarks on representative inputs measure the overall inference speed and efficiency of the system.

- **Clear Separation:** The separation is maintained by:

    -  Explicitly documented assumptions and boundaries for each component.
    -   Independent numerical references and fault injection techniques used for testing, but not integrated into the core execution path.
    -  A focus on measuring and documenting the impact of changes on the "real" production performance.

**Key Correctness Contracts:**

The README highlights three crucial correctness contracts:

1. **Lossless Probability Correction:**  The speculative decoding mechanism (H1) must preserve the original target probability distribution, ensuring the generated text remains consistent with the model's intended output. This is validated through analytical tests and careful implementation.
2. **Packed Projections and Fused Sums:**  The engine must correctly handle packed weight projections and fused activation sums, ensuring efficient memory utilization and accurate calculations.  Metal numerical tests verify the correctness of these operations.
3. **Target Equations and Cache Management:** The core target execution logic must adhere to the Gemma 3 model's equations and manage local caches correctly. Tests ensure that the target calculations are accurate and that cache operations are consistent.

 **Limitations:**

- **macOS Only:** Guffin is currently designed for macOS and M4 chip architecture.
- **Limited Model Support:** The project primarily supports Gemma 3 and 2 models with limited support for other models.
- **Benchmarking Still Pending:** While the README outlines performance targets, release benchmarks and comparisons to other inference engines are not yet available.



**Overall:**

Guffin presents a well-structured and promising approach to native inference on macOS. Its modular design, emphasis on correctness through rigorous testing, and focus on performance optimization make it a valuable contribution to the open-source machine learning community.

**Before Committing:**

**1. Understand the Contract:**

- **Read `ENGINE_PRINCIPLES.md`:**  Focus on ownership, layout, lifetime, synchronization, and correctness invariants for tensors, buffers, and caches.
- **Review `README.md`:**  Especially the sections on lossless sampling, packed projections, and target equations.

**2. Automated Correctness Checks:**

- **Run Unit Tests:** Ensure your changes pass all existing tests in `tests/engine/` and `tests/tensor/`.

- **Targeted Numerical Tests:**

    - For projections & sums: `tests/tensor/gemma3_metal_tests.cpp`

- **Validate Assumptions:** Use independent references or parity tests to check numerical correctness of your changes.

**3. Actual Chat Performance:**

- **Build Release Version:**  Ensure your build is optimized for production execution.
- **Consistent Environment:** Control system state (thermals, memory pressure) and use the same model, context, and prompt for all runs.
- **Warm Up:** Run a few iterations before taking measurements.
- **Multiple Runs:** Repeat measurements multiple times and report variance.
- **Compare to Baseline:** Measure the impact of your changes on `generation tok/s` and `internal TTFT` compared to the existing baseline.

**4. Document Your Changes:**

- Explain your design choices in code comments.
- Clearly state any assumptions made and their impact.
- Provide a summary of the performance gains (or losses) observed.
